code: What Do We Do in Science?

items.text:
Welcome students to the class. Ask them about the most "boring" thing they did today. 

Do not agree or disagree with them. This is just to have a light-hearted moment with the students.
Then, tell them that you have an interesting game to play.

items.name: heavy-bag
items.html:
Weighings: 0
Put the same number of bags on each pan, then press Weigh.

items.text:
Narrate: There are nine bags. Eight bags have the same weight, and one bag is heavier than the rest.

Spot the heavier bag using only two weighings.
Show students the mechanics of the game by solving the puzzle incorrectly. Do this as quickly as possible.

Ask students to think about its solution. Give them only 1 minute.

Give the simulation's access to the student who says they have solved it.

Let them demonstrate the solution by interacting with the simulation. 

If nobody has solved it, demonstrate the solution. The idea is to weigh only six weights, three on the left and three on the right, in the first weighing.

script.x:
Learn these game mechanics before the class: 

You may drag and drop the weights onto the pan. Clicking on a weight that is already on the pan will drop it from the pan.

A pan can hold at most 4 weights.

Clicking on "I know which one" will let you choose the bag that you think is heavier, and will tell you whether you are right.

Clicking on "New puzzle" will reset the puzzle, and might change the number of the heavier bag.

items.text: Ask this: Since the weights alone do not help us find the max. weight that the handle holds, do you think these new items, commonly found in school, will help us?

Give a student access to this simulation, and let them and the class play around to find the max. weight that the handle holds.

Let this happen for at most 5 minutes. Then, proceed to the first "Ask/Discuss."

Proceed to the second "Ask/Discuss."

Give a student access to this simulation, and let them and the class play around to answer the question.

They must realise that no strap ever tears. So, we must think of a new experiment.

Before going ahead, ask students to guess the exact max. loads for each: one strap and both straps.

Get the class to agree on only one number for each. Write down that number on this screen.

script.x:
Learn these new game mechanics before the class: Clicking on "+" beside any item adds 1 of it to the bag.

On the left of the boy, you can see the items currently in the bag and their multipliers. Clicking on one of the items reduces its number in the bag by 1.
What is the max. weight that the handle holds?
script.a:
Students must find that at 6 notes, 43 texts, and 1 geometry box, the handle tears (18.01 Kg). 

But the handle holds 5 notes, 44 texts, and 1 geometry box (18.00 Kg). So, 18.00 Kg is the max. load that the handle holds.

script.x: What is the maximum weight that one strap or both straps hold?

items.text:
Say that a new device is needed to perform the next experiment: a spring balance. 

Introduce students to it by hanging objects from it and measuring their weights.

items.name: spring-balance

items.text:
Introduce students to this setup, where a loaded bag is hung from a spring balance.

Start spinning but do not go all the way to the tearing point of any strap. Students will see that the spring balance reading has changed.
Give one student access to this simulation (One Strap). Ask them to start spinning and interact with the slider. They and the class must find the max. load that one strap holds. Record this reading.

Give another student access to this simulation (Both Straps). Ask them to start spinning and interact with the slider. They and the class must find the max. load that both straps hold. Record this reading.

Proceed to the first "Ask/Discuss."

The answer to this will depend on the guesses.

Proceed to the second "Ask/Discuss."

The answer to this will depend on the guesses.

Tell the class to summarise the max. load that each of the following holds: the handle, one strap, and both the straps. 

Write them down on this screen.

script.x: Did our guesses match the results of our experiments?
What does this say about our guesses?

items.title: Key point
items.content:
Observation is the first step in doing science.

Observation can build curiosity, which can make us ask questions.

items.text: Proceed to "Ask/Discuss."
Reveal the key point and read it as it is soon after the expected answer to "Ask/Discuss" is revealed.

script.x: We spent quite sometime discussing about a bag. How did that start?
script.a:
We saw that the handle could hold the purple weight, but not the weight of both purple and black. 

So, there must be a max. weight that the handle holds. This made us question what the handle's max. holding weight is, which   started our investigation.

That said, it all started with us "observing" or seeing what happened to the bag.

items.text:
Remind students about the guesses they took during the class, and before the experiments. 

This is the next step in doing science: guessing.
Proceed to "Ask/Discuss."

items.title: Key point
items.content: A guess cannot never be wrong! In science, a guess must be able to be proven false by an experiment or observation.

items.text: Reveal the key point and read it as it is soon after the expected answer to "Ask/Discuss" is revealed.

script.x: What if we did not guess the exact number for the max. load of the handle, but instead guessed that the max. load it holds is a small number?
script.a:
Then, whatever the test result is, you can keep the guess alive. 

18 kg? Small compared to a car. 
0.2 kg? Small compared to almost anything. There is no result that forces you to give up the guess.

items.text: Lastly, recall the results of all the tests done in the class, and say whether they matched the guesses. This is the next step in doing science: testing.
Proceed to "Ask/Discuss."
Reveal the key point and read it as it is soon after the expected answer to "Ask/Discuss" is revealed.

Summarise: So, doing science starts with observing the world around us, asking questions about what we saw, then making guesses that can be proven wrong, and finally testing to see whether the guesses were right.

Say this: Now that we have done some experiments, can you think like a scientist?

This is said to transition to the quiz in the next section.

items.title: Key point
items.content: If our guess disagrees with the result of the test, then our guess is wrong.

script.x: If the results of the test disagree with the guess, what can we say about the guess?
script.a: The guess is wrong, provided our test was done carefully.

script.x:
If asked about what a careful test is, tell them that if the spring balance and the weighing scale in our experiments were faulty, we would not have gotten the true value for the max. loads. 

In all our experiments, we assumed that our devices were working properly.

items.text:
Ask students to just "see" what you are doing. 

Hit "Tare," and then make the boy hold the bag by its handle. Place the purple weight into the bag and then the black one. The handle must tear after the black one is placed.

Reset, and repeat the activity with one strap around the boy. The strap survives. Then, place the brown weight and the strap tears.  

Lastly, reset and repeat the previous activity with both straps around the boy. The straps survive. Then, place the red weight and the straps tear.
Proceed to the first "Ask/Discuss" that is on your right, under "Teacher Note."

Proceed to the second "Ask/Discuss." 

For this, give the simulation's access to a student, and let them and the class figure out the answer.

Let them play around for 3 - 4 minutes.

Proceed to the third "Ask/Discuss." 

The answer to this question will be revealed during the class.

Before going ahead, get students to guess the exact number for the max. weight that the handle holds. 

Get the class to agree on only one number. Write down that number on this screen.

Later, the tests will reveal whether they were right or wrong.

script.x:
Learn these game mechanics before the class:

The button in the top right corner resets the simulation.

Each of the three buttons in the top left corner makes the boy put on the bag in a certain manner. This changes the weighing scale reading since the bag weighs 0.60 Kg.

Clicking on "Tare" brings the weighing scale reading to 0 Kg. Use this to find the actual load on the bag's handle or straps.

You may drag and drop weights into the bag. A bag can hold at most five weights.

On the boy's left, you will see the weights in the bag. Clicking on any one weight will drop it from the bag.
What does this activity tell you about the bag?
script.a:
For any given part of the bag (handle, one strap or both straps), there are some weights that it can hold, but add more weights to the bag, and the part tears.

So, for every part, there is a max. weight that it holds. If you add to that weight, the part tears.

script.x: What do you think is the maximum weight that the handle holds?
script.a:
This simulation cannot help us find this value. 

14.60 Kg is the greatest weight at which the handle survives, and 21.60 Kg is the least weight at which we see the handle torn. 

So, the max. load could be somewhere between these two values, or 14.60 Kg itself (not 21.60 Kg).

script.x: Then, how do we find the maximum weight that the handle holds?

chunks.name: Can You Think Like a Scientist?

items.prompt: Two groups test the tearing point of the same handle. One gets 18.01 kg, the other 17.60 kg. What should happen next?
options: Trust the first group, they went first
Find out what each group did differently

items.prompt: A group predicts the handle breaks at 25 kg. It breaks at 18 Kg. What have they got?
options: A useful result, since a wrong guess still rules something out
Nothing, they should have guessed better

items.prompt: A group tests one bag and reports "school bags do not tear at 18 kg." What's the flaw?
options: One bag can't speak for all bags
18 kg is too small to matter

items.prompt: Someone says "heavier bags break handles faster." Why is that hard to test?
options: The meaning of "faster" is not exact in this discussion, so no result could settle it

items.prompt: A group repeats the same test five times and gets 18.01 kg every time. What does that prove?
options: The test is repeatable, which isn't the same as correct
Five times is enough for anything
